n: A new message comes in the form of a riddle—an allegory about eagles, a cedar, and a vine.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

n: Ezekiel is to pose a riddle and tell a parable. Its meaning is explained in verses 11–21.

f.g: Hebrew ḥidah—a puzzling saying that needs interpretation.

n: A magnificent eagle (Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon) comes to Lebanon and takes the top of a cedar. The cedar represents the royal house of David in Jerusalem.

f.g: Famous for cedars; here symbolizing Jerusalem, whose palace was built of Lebanese cedar.

n: He snaps off the topmost shoot—King Jehoiachin—and carries it to a land of trade, a city of merchants: Babylon.

f.g: A land of trade—Babylon (literally “the land of Canaan,” here meaning “merchant land”).

n: He takes a native seedling—Zedekiah, a member of the royal family—and plants it in fertile soil by abundant water.
It grows into a low, spreading vine whose branches turn toward the eagle—a lesser kingdom loyal to Babylon.

f.w: a spreading vine of low stature
f.g: Judah as a humble vassal state, not a towering cedar.

n: A second great eagle appears—Pharaoh of Egypt—and the vine bends its roots and branches toward him for water. Zedekiah turned to Egypt for help against Babylon.
Yet the vine had already been planted in good soil with plenty of water. It had everything it needed to flourish where it was.

f.w: planted in a good soil by great waters
f.g: Under Babylon’s rule Judah could have survived peacefully.

n: Will it thrive? No—it will be uprooted and its fruit stripped, and it will wither, easily pulled up.

f.w: shall he not pull up the roots thereof
f.g: Babylon will uproot the disloyal vine.

n: When the hot east wind blows, it will dry up right where it grew. The east wind symbolizes Babylon.

f.g: A scorching desert wind; an image of destruction from the east.

n: God now explains the riddle.

f.w: Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me

n: Don’t you understand? The king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and took its king and nobles to Babylon in 597 BC.
He made a covenant with a member of the royal family (Zedekiah) and put him under oath, taking away the nation’s strongest men.

f.w: hath taken an oath of him
f.g: Zedekiah swore loyalty in God’s name.

n: Babylon intended Judah to be a humble kingdom that would survive by keeping that treaty.
But Zedekiah rebelled, sending envoys to Egypt for horses and troops. Can someone break a sworn covenant and escape?
God swears that Zedekiah will die in Babylon, the land of the king whose oath he despised. This was fulfilled.

f.w: in the midst of Babylon he shall die

n: Pharaoh’s great army will be of no help when Babylon builds siege works against Jerusalem.

f.w: Neither shall Pharaoh with his mighty army

n: Because Zedekiah gave his hand in pledge and then broke the oath, he will not escape. Promises matter to God, even ones made to pagans.

f.g: Shaken hands in a binding pledge.

n: The oath was sworn in the Lord’s name, so God calls it “mine oath” and “my covenant.” Breaking it was breaking faith with God himself.

f.w: mine oath that he hath despised

n: God will catch Zedekiah in his net and bring him to Babylon to be judged for this betrayal.

f.w: I will spread my net upon him

n: His fleeing troops will fall by the sword and the rest will be scattered—exactly as happened in 586 BC.

A messianic promise follows: God himself will take a tender shoot from the top of the cedar—David’s line—and plant it on a high mountain. Latter-day Saint readers have also noted the parallel with Mulek, a young son of Zedekiah whom the Lord led to the Americas.

f.w: I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar

n: Planted on Israel’s high mountain, it will become a majestic cedar sheltering birds of every kind—a picture of the Messiah’s kingdom welcoming all peoples. Jesus used similar imagery for the kingdom of God.

f.w: the mountain of the height of Israel
under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing

n: All nations will see that God brings down the proud and lifts up the humble, withers the green and makes the dry flourish. What God says, he does.

f.w: have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree
